meta.title: Tasks. Frame and Run — course 1 · AIVIS.ONE
meta.desc: A free AIVIS.ONE course: how to set tasks for a chat, check answers and lead big tasks.
s01.t03: In one hour you will learn to
s01.t04: set a task for a chat in four parts
s01.t05: check an answer as deeply as a mistake would cost
s01.t06: break a big task into steps and start a new chat in time
s02.t02: Time shrinks: what took a day now takes minutes
s02.t03: Understand a topic: minutes instead of days
s02.t04: Write a document: minutes instead of hours
s02.t05: Gather and compare options: a couple of minutes instead of a day
s02.t06: The course goes step by step: how the model (the program that writes the chat's answers) works, how to set a task, how to check, how to run big tasks. One example all the way: a book exchange, the announcement and the event plan.
s03.t02: Not a wizard: a probability machine
s03.t03: Text is cut into small pieces called tokens.
s03.t04: Inside there are no words or meanings, only odds: which piece follows which.
s03.t05: Each time it adds the most likely continuation, like phone autocomplete with trillions of examples.
s03.t06: It is not a reference book or a smart search. What you put in decides what comes out.
s04.t02: One question, different answers. It is not a fault
s04.t03: A new chat is a blank sheet: it does not remember the last task and starts from zero.
s04.t04: Memory (if on) keeps general facts about you, not the content of earlier chats.
s04.t05: A different chat, file or wording gives a different result.
s04.t06: Control the input and the output becomes predictable.
s05.t02: Context is a table. What is not on the table does not exist for the model.
s05.t04: On the table: the model sees it
s05.t10: Off the table: not there for the model
s05.t13: A file you did not attach
s05.t14: You know the book exchange is on Saturday. If you did not write it, for the model there is no Saturday exchange.
s06.t02: One word, different meanings: keep your own glossary
s06.t05: The model may read it as
s06.t07: a meeting where people swap books
s06.l02: The model may read it as
s06.t10: a line about one book in a list
s06.l04: The model may read it as
s06.t11: a bank card or a playing card
s06.l06: The model may read it as
s06.t15: Pick 5 to 7 of your words: what they mean for you and what they do not. Paste them at the start of the chat.
s07.t04: Context: everything that must be on the table: who, when, files, from whose point of view.
s07.t05: Format: what the result looks like: length, tone, structure.
s07.t06: Constraints: what not to do and what is out of scope.
s07.t07: A point of view in the context replaces the line “act as an expert”.
s08.t02: A weak request and a strong one: four parts
s08.t05: You get a generic template that you will have to rewrite.
s08.t08: invite 20 people to the book exchange
s08.t10: neighbours and colleagues; Saturday at 12:00; bring one to three books you are happy to give away
s08.t15: Add one line: “Ask me clarifying questions” and the model will ask instead of guessing.
s09.t02: Why the model rushes and flatters
s09.t03: It rushes: a fast, confident answer beats a question back.
s09.t04: The cost: the answer looks fine but misses the request, and time goes on redoing it.
s09.t05: It flatters: “great question” is not an independent verdict on your idea.
s09.t06: Say once how to work with you, and from then on it applies by itself.
s10.t02: A short chat setup (text to paste)
s10.t03: A prompt is the text you give a chat. Paste it once into the chat settings section where you can say how to work with you. From then on it applies in every chat. The text stays in English; the chat will still answer in your language. Try it: give any task and the chat asks questions first.
s10.p01:
You are my working assistant. Follow these rules in every reply:

- Be concise. No filler, no flattery, no "happy to help".
- Don't pad answers with caveats, disclaimers, or unrequested suggestions.
- Don't repeat my question back to me.
- Before doing any non-trivial task, ask me clarifying questions if anything is unclear. Don't guess.
- If you're not sure about a fact, say so plainly instead of inventing it.
- Do only what I asked. If you think something extra is worth doing, mention it in one line at the end, don't just do it.
s11.t02: Have it retell the task before it works
s11.t05: The model silently writes a plan for the wrong event.
s11.t07: “Before you start, tell me how you understood the task and what you are going to do”
s11.t08: Model: “I understood: I write an announcement.” You: “No, I need a plan on a page.” Caught in ten seconds.
s11.t09: Ten seconds of checking save half an hour of work off target.
s12.t02: Precise words, dialogue, options with reasons
s12.t07: “Five lines, no exclamation marks” instead of “make it good”
s12.t08: “Good” is not a format: the model guesses
s12.t10: “Shorten it”, “add time and place”, “drop the second paragraph”
s12.t11: The first answer is a rough version; edits are normal
s12.t13: “Give 2–3 options, pros and cons of each, and your recommendation”
s12.t14: You grasp the choice instead of guessing
s13.t02: workit: our file of ready-made working rules for any chat
s13.t03: One plain text file: open it, copy it and paste it at the start of a chat, and the chat works by the rules
s13.t04: A goal, and how you will know it is done
s13.t05: Stays on goal: the chat does not drift
s13.t07: A map of the work: what is done and what is next
s14.t02: What not to paste and what to check in your chat settings
s14.t04: Passwords for services and sites, text-message codes
s14.t06: Other people's personal data and private material you may not share
s14.t08: Names become “Person A”, sums become “about N”, remove addresses and numbers
s14.t09: Read the text yourself before you send it
s14.t10: For sensitive things, use a private chat without history
s14.t11: What to check in the settings. In the data settings, find three things: whether the service uses your conversations to keep training its model, and how to switch that off; how long deleted chats are kept; whether temporary (incognito) chats without history are offered. Every service has its own rules and they change, so read them for the one you use.
s15.t03: The model does not feel the line between knowing and guessing: the tone is the same.
s15.t04: The invention looks the way you expect: numbers, quotes, links.
s15.t05: A case, 2025. A large consulting firm delivered a report to a government with references to research that does not exist and an invented quote from a court ruling. A researcher noticed, the report was corrected and part of the fee was refunded. Even professionals must check.
s15.t06: Source: AP news report, 7 October 2025
s16.t02: The cost of a mistake sets how deep you check
s16.t07: Everyday tasks: a sketch of the announcement
s16.t08: A sceptic's stance: assume mistakes exist, list them, fix them
s16.t10: Work documents: the event plan on a page
s16.t11: Re-read from the top, check against what was agreed, an honest “needs checking” mark
s16.t13: Responsible material: the announcement everyone will see
s16.t14: A list of every claim, a mark of how important each problem found is (course 2 uses three: SERIOUS, MISSED, MINOR), up to three rounds of checking
s16.t15: Red flags: too smooth; an exact number with no source; “as is known…”; the answer matches what you hoped to hear.
s17.t02: Did it read the whole file?
s17.t03: With a long file the model often reads the start and the end and skips the middle. Upload the file and paste this prompt. Instead of “are you sure?” ask: “What is this based on? Give a source” and “Name 2–3 weak points”.
s17.p01:
I've uploaded a file. Before you analyze or summarize anything, I need you to actually read all of it — beginning, middle, and end — not just the start and finish.

Write me a "full-read report" that proves you went through the whole document:
- Confirm you read it completely, top to bottom.
- Briefly state what's covered in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end (name specific sections or page numbers from the middle, so it's clear the middle wasn't skipped).
- Flag anything that looks cut off, missing, or inconsistent.

Only after this report do the task I actually need.
s18.t02: Politeness does not work: ask for checkable actions
s18.t04: “Try hard, be careful, don't make mistakes”
s18.t05: The model says “sure” and writes just as confidently.
s18.t08: “Quote verbatim the lines your conclusion rests on”
s18.t10: “A source for every figure; without one write ‘not confirmed’”
s18.t13: Ask for actions that cannot be faked, not for effort.
s19.t03: Plan: “Do not do it yet. Write the plan: 5–7 steps, order, result.”
s19.t04: Edit: you read the plan as the person who knows the situation.
s19.t05: Steps: do, show, check, go on. A mistake in step one does not reach step seven.
s19.t06: A short brief: goal; what is in; what is out; how we will check the result.
s19.t07: The book exchange: venue, announcement, book list, schedule, tidy-up, one step at a time.
s20.t02: A research chat for fresh data
s20.t03: Fetch fresh data in a separate chat where internet search is turned on (switch it on in the chat settings or with a button by the input box; if there is none, this service cannot search) and bring only the short digest back to the main chat. Replace the [brackets] with your topic.
s20.p01:
Act as a research assistant with web search turned on. I need fresh, current information on the topic below, and I'll move your result into another chat — so give me a clean digest, not raw search clutter.

TOPIC: [describe what you need: the question, the time frame, why it matters]

RULES
- Use web search. Don't rely on what you "already know" — my topic needs current data.
- Before searching, tell me in one line what exactly you're looking for and how you'll filter results. Then search.
- Prefer reliable, primary sources. Skip low-quality or unverifiable ones.
- For every key fact, note where it came from, so I can trust it.

RETURN ONLY THIS (no search dump):
- A short, structured digest of the findings, in my own words.
- Key facts with their sources.
- Anything that's contested or uncertain, flagged as such.
- A one-paragraph bottom line I can paste straight into my main chat.
s21.t02: A tired chat is not healed, it is moved
s21.t03: Signs: it answers something else, blends old and new, returns to what you cancelled, repeats itself. Do not coax it. Ask for a hand-over summary (snapshot), open a new chat, paste it there.
s21.p01:
This chat is getting long and starting to lose the thread. I want to move our work to a fresh chat without losing anything.

Write me a compact handoff summary I can paste into a new chat to continue seamlessly. Include:
- The task: what we're working on and the goal.
- Key decisions and conclusions reached so far.
- Final wording / results we've already locked in (quote them exactly).
- What's still left to do.
- Any essential context the new chat needs to pick up where we left off.

Keep it tight and dense — no fluff, no retelling the whole conversation. Just what a fresh chat needs to continue as if it had been here the whole time.
s22.t02: Your own task: the whole cycle, step by step
s22.t03: Task: take your own, a real one.
s22.t04: Formula: Goal, Context, Format, Constraints, plus “Ask me clarifying questions”.
s22.t05: Test = test: have it retell the task, correct it.
s22.t06: Work: a big one by plan and in steps.
s22.t07: Check: depth by the cost of a mistake; chat tired, move it.
s22.t08: Beginner mistakes: everything in one message; the first answer as final; arguing in a tired chat; no check.
s23.t06: Chat setup, test = test, options, checks, hand-over summary, research.
s23.t07: Download all the prompts as one archive (.zip: opens with a double click)
s23.t11: Have it retell the task before it works.
s23.t13: Depth of checking follows the cost of a mistake.
